extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology, literary criticism, and humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and describing technical means by which wit is produced (logical faults, linguistic devices, allusion, substitution, etc.), illustrated with literary and anecdotal examples. Useful for scholars, critics, or writers studying mechanisms of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophistical faulty thinking (omission / contradictory separate assertions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A speaker makes several separate assertions which are individually plausible but together mutually exclude each other; treats what must be taken as a whole as isolated parts (e.g., kettle defense: 'I never borrowed it; it had a hole when I received it; it was perfect when I returned it').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: the comic/witty effect arises from the logical incompatibility revealed when the parts are (implicitly) combined. Example: the kettle story. Anti-pattern: presenting contradictions calmly so the audience doesn't notice the mutual exclusion. Use to expose self-contradiction by letting each assertion seem reasonable in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equating possibility with actuality (possibility treated as equivalent to reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuing a mere possibility as if it were an accomplished fact; the speaker displaces attention from actual condition to hypothetical scenarios (e.g., marriage-agent arguing a short-legged bride is safer because she can't become lame later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: comic effect comes from the absurd transfer of weight from actuality to improbable possibilities. Example: telepathic Rabbi story and the marriage-agent insisting on the 'finished misfortune' as preferable. Use to satirize exaggerated hypothetical reasoning; avoid when truth/precision is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic errors of thought (automatism / echoing habit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated, automatic reactions (habitual echoing or reinforcement) that fail to adapt to a changed context and thereby betray the speaker’s intention (e.g., assistant echoing praise then echoing a conceded defect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: produce comedy by showing how habit/automatism overrides situational judgment. Examples: the echoing assistant; agent who blurts an incriminating corroboration. Use to reveal self-betrayal; important element for comic unmasking. Anti-pattern: making repetitions obviously staged rather than seemingly unconscious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification (establishing unexpected identity between relations/definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forming a new, unexpected identity or parallelism between two relations or definitions so that two similar relationships are expressed together (e.g., 'Human life is divided into two halves; during the first one looks forward to the second, and during the second one looks backward to the first').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: create wit by recognizing and stating a similarity of relations (not just words). Examples: Lichtenberg's 'January...' and the 'two halves of human life'. Furnishes basis for repartee and 'turning the tables.' Distinguish from mere repetition or double-meaning: unification links relations, not just wordplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repartee (turning the tables / using defense for aggression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ready retort that uses the opponent’s attack as basis for a counter-attack, establishing an unexpected identity between attack and counter-attack (e.g., baker/tavern-keeper exchange).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: quick, context-aware inversion of an opponent’s thrust. Example: 'You got into my beer' / 'One of your rolls got under my fingernail.' Use for sharp, immediate wit in dialogue. Requires brevity, speed, and intelligible role-reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witty enumeration / coordination (addition of 'and' to signal relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a coordinated list and especially the placement of 'and' to imply a surprising or emphatic relation among items (e.g., Heine's 'students, professors, Philistines, and cattle' where 'and' stresses an intended equivalence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: produce wit by arranging items so that the middle element changes interpretation of the others; use conjunction placement to dramatize an implied relation. Example contrasts with mere comical aggregation (fork + effort example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation through the opposite
rubrics_metrics.description: A substitution of the opposite answer or description for the expected one (e.g., answering 'Yes, but they won't come' to the question 'Can you call up ghosts?'), often producing irony or satirical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: say the opposite (sometimes with a qualifying 'but') so that the literal phrasing becomes equivalent to the denied answer; creates irony when audience reads the contradiction. Examples: Frederick the Great/clairvoyant anecdote. Note: this is also the central technique of irony more generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outdoing wit (contradiction as exaggerated confirmation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing the appropriate mild answer with a contradiction that, by context, functions as a stronger affirmation or rebuttal (e.g., professor asks if the king commands amputation of the other leg after royal praise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: exaggerate by using contrarian phrasing which intensifies the intended meaning. Examples: Lessing epigram, Jewish bathing quips, the surgical-clinic anecdote. Use to amplify sarcasm or expose absurdity; related to representation through the opposite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect expression / Allusion (representation via associations and relationships)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressing a disallowed or delicate meaning indirectly by invoking an associated situation, phrase, or image that the audience will infer (e.g., pointing to the empty space between two portraits and asking 'And where is the Savior?' to imply the sitters are thieves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: employ associations (sound, sentence structure, cultural images) to suggest a forbidden or impolite judgment without stating it. Varieties include sound similarity, sentence-structure imitation, and conceptual parallels. Examples: 'New baths heal well' (alluding to 'New brooms...'), 'The trip around the Wilt' pun. Useful for polite irony or insistent insinuation; requires shared cultural references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allusion by modification (sound/phrase alteration and minor changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating wit by slightly altering a familiar phrase or word (letter change, pun-like tweak) so the audience recalls the original and perceives the satirical target (e.g., 'the trip around the Wilt' or 'every fathom a queen').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: minimal changes to a well-known formula produce cognitive linkage and comic meaning. Examples: 'Mellingitis' (allusion to meningitis), 'un_believer Spinoza.' Use for economical and pointed jests; risk: if modification is too obscure, audience misses the allusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission as allusion (omission without substitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaving out a connecting thought or key phrase so the audience must infer the intended meaning; the gap functions as the wit (e.g., 'When X. hears this he will receive another box on his ear' implying that X will respond with a caustic article).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: imply the rest of the reasoning rather than stating it; the audience supplies the omitted link, producing the comic effect. Examples: Heine's 'pastils for fumigation' remark; the umbrella-wife proverb. Use to hint at taboo or complex ideas economically; avoid over-elliptical omission that leaves readers confused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation through the minute or minutest element
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterizing an entire situation or person by concentrating on a trivial or minute detail that reveals the larger truth (e.g., Jew on train quickly replacing feet on seat when asked about Yom Kippur; progressive cries of a woman in labor yield information about timing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: spotlight a small, telling sign that stands for the whole; comedic effect comes from sudden transfer of importance to the minute. Examples noted above. Use to dramatize economy of expression and the revealing power of tiny facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manifold application of the same material / condensation by repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the same word or construction in multiple related senses (parallelism or condensation) to create wit through repetition or double meaning (e.g., 'Experience consists in experiencing what one does not care to experience').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: reuse linguistic material in overlapping senses; can verge on punning or tautology but becomes witty when relationships between senses are illuminating. Distinguish from pure double-meaning: here the same material is applied to parallel relations. Use for epigrammatic observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison-wit (representation via analogy or simile)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using comparison or simile to evoke wit by equating unlike things in a way that produces an ironic or surprising insight (the text notes this is common but technically complex and ambiguous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: craft comparisons that reveal a hidden likeness or ironic contrast. The author warns that classifying some comparisons as witty is uncertain; use comparison carefully because it can be comic rather than strictly witty. Further analysis required to separate comic from witty comparisons.
